context.heading: God visited the house of bread
context.body: Naomi hears that the LORD had paqad ("attended to" or "visited") His people by giving them food. The verb is used when God steps in to act, as in Genesis 50:24 and Exodus 3:16. There is irony here: Bethlehem means "house of bread", and famine had emptied it.

context.heading: Holding on like a spouse
context.body: Orpah kisses Naomi goodbye, but Ruth davaq ("clung") to her. It is the same verb Genesis 2:24 uses for a husband who holds fast to his wife. Ruth's words in verses 16–17 are a covenant oath, sealed with a self-curse, not a sentimental farewell.

context.heading: Bitter, and blaming the Almighty
context.body: Naomi renames herself Mara ("bitter") and says Shaddai ("the Almighty") has dealt bitterly with her. Shaddai is the name God used with the patriarchs (Genesis 17:1). She is right that God is sovereign. She is wrong that He is finished: she says she came back empty while Ruth stands beside her.

theology.title: God in the ordinary
theology.body: Ruth has no miracles, visions or prophets. The narrator says outright that God acted only twice, here in 1:6 and again in 4:13. Yet the whole book is His work, carried out through famine, funerals and family decisions. He is the God who governs history from inside everyday life.

theology.title: Room for an outsider
theology.body: Moab was Israel's old rival, and the Law limited Moabites' place in Israel's assembly (Deuteronomy 23:3). Yet Ruth says, "your God will be my God." From the start God promised to bless all nations through Abraham (Genesis 12:3), and Ruth is an early picture of outsiders brought near (Ephesians 2:12–13).

theology.title: Lament is not unbelief
theology.body: Naomi's complaint in verses 20–21 is never rebuked by the narrator. Like Job and many psalms, she brings raw grief straight to God and names Him as the one responsible. The Bible makes space for honest bitterness spoken toward God rather than away from Him.

application.title: Loyalty that costs something
application.body: Ruth chose a grieving mother-in-law, a foreign country and probable poverty. Loyalty is easy when it pays. Hers had no visible reward.
application.question: Who in your life needs you to stay when leaving would be easier?

application.title: Don't rename yourself too soon
application.body: Naomi called herself Bitter while the answer to her grief was standing next to her. Grief narrows what we can see. That is human, but it is not the final word.
application.question: What label have you put on your life that might be premature?

application.title: Coming home empty
application.body: Naomi did not pretend. She walked back into town and admitted she had lost everything, and the whole town saw it.
application.question: Where do you need to let your church or family see you come back empty?

context.heading: A worthy man, a worthy woman
context.body: Boaz is called a man of chayil, a word for strength, wealth and worth together. In 3:11 Boaz calls Ruth a woman of chayil, the same phrase as Proverbs 31:10. In many Hebrew Bibles, Ruth comes right after Proverbs, as if to show the ideal woman alive in a Moabite widow.

context.heading: Noticed though foreign
context.body: Ruth asks why Boaz would "take notice" of her, since she is a nokhriyah, "a foreigner". In Hebrew the two words sound alike and share a root. Her question is essentially: why would anyone see someone people are trained to look past?

context.heading: Real danger in the field
context.body: Boaz orders his young men not to touch Ruth (v. 9), and Naomi later warns her to stay out of other fields (v. 22). Harvest fields could be unsafe for a woman alone and without family. Boaz's protection is not a romantic flourish but practical justice for the vulnerable.

theology.title: Providence with a smile
theology.body: Ruth "happened" into the right field, and "just then" Boaz arrived (v. 4). The narrator never says God arranged it; he lets readers notice. Scripture often shows God steering through ordinary choices (Proverbs 16:9), working all things for His people's good (Romans 8:28).

theology.title: Mercy above the minimum
theology.body: The gleaning law set a floor. Boaz goes far past it: water, a seat at his meal, and grain dropped on purpose for her (vv. 14–16). His generosity reflects the God of Israel, who gives more than the law requires and loves the foreigner (Deuteronomy 10:18–19).

theology.title: Loyal love has not stopped
theology.body: When Naomi hears Boaz's name, she blesses the LORD, whose chesed has not left "the living or the dead" (v. 20). Then she says the key word: he is one of our goel, our redeemers. Her hope begins to return.

application.title: Margins on purpose
application.body: The gleaning law built generosity into the business model: farmers left profit in the field on purpose. Generosity was planned, not leftover.
application.question: What part of your income or calendar is deliberately left for someone else?

application.title: Reputation goes ahead of you
application.body: Boaz had heard how Ruth treated Naomi before he ever met her (v. 11). Her quiet faithfulness at home became her introduction.
application.question: If someone asked around about you, what would they hear about how you treat your own family?

application.title: Ask whose she is
application.body: Boaz's first question is "Whose young woman is this?" He noticed a stranger on the edges and asked about her.
application.question: Who on the edges of your workplace or church has nobody asked about yet?

context.heading: Night at the threshing floor
context.body: Grain was winnowed in the evening breeze on a goren ("threshing floor"), a hard, open patch of ground. After the work, men ate, celebrated the harvest and slept beside the grain to guard it. The setting gave Ruth a private moment to make a request that would shame no one if refused.

context.heading: The place of his feet
context.body: Ruth uncovers Boaz's margelot, "the place of his feet". Because "feet" is sometimes a euphemism elsewhere, some readers hear sexual overtones. The text itself presents both as people of integrity (vv. 11, 14), and most interpreters see a humble, symbolic posture: she lies down as a petitioner, and what she asks for is marriage, settled publicly the next day.

context.heading: A nearer redeemer
context.body: Boaz says yes, but admits there is a closer goel ("kinsman-redeemer"). The right to redeem went in order of nearness (Leviticus 25:48–49). Boaz will not cut a corner, even for something he clearly wants.

theology.title: God answers through courage
theology.body: In 2:12 Boaz prayed God would reward Ruth. Now Ruth asks Boaz to be part of that answer. God's providence does not cancel bold human action; it usually works through it, as with Esther (Esther 4:14).

theology.title: Kindness that mirrors God
theology.body: Boaz calls Ruth's request a greater chesed than her first. She chose an older relative to protect Naomi's family line rather than pursuing a younger man for herself. Her loyal love echoes God's own character (Exodus 34:6).

theology.title: The Redeemer who pays
theology.body: The prophets later call God Himself Israel's goel (Isaiah 41:14; 54:5). The New Testament presents Christ as the Redeemer who paid the price with His own blood (1 Peter 1:18–19; Galatians 4:4–5). Boaz is a small picture: a willing relative who will bear the cost.

application.title: Ask clearly
application.body: Ruth did not hint or manipulate. She said plainly what she wanted and why she had a right to ask.
application.question: What request are you hinting at instead of asking plainly?

application.title: Integrity at night
application.body: Boaz could have taken advantage in the dark. Instead he protected Ruth's name (v. 14) and kept the process honest.
application.question: What shortcut are you tempted to take in private that you would never take in public?

application.title: Wait after you act
application.body: "Wait, my daughter," Naomi says (v. 18). After bold action comes the harder part: not refreshing the screen every five minutes.
application.question: Where have you done your part and now need to let it rest?

context.heading: Acquiring a name
context.body: Boaz says he has qanah ("acquired" or "bought") the land and Ruth as his wife, "to raise up the name of the deceased" (v. 10). It is legal language for taking on a guardian's duty. The nearer relative backs out because it would jeopardize his own inheritance (v. 6); Boaz takes on cost, not profit.

context.heading: Sealed with a sandal
context.body: Handing over a na'al ("sandal") confirmed the transfer, since walking on land was a picture of owning it (Joshua 1:3). The narrator explains the custom as old, so the book was probably written down some time after these events. Deuteronomy 25:9 records a harsher, shaming version of the same practice.

context.heading: The family of Perez
context.body: The elders bless Boaz with a house like that of Perez, born to Tamar and Judah (Genesis 38). Tamar was another outsider widow whose determination kept a family line alive. Bethlehem's clan descended from Perez (v. 18), so the blessing ties Ruth into a pattern God had used before.

theology.title: Empty to full
theology.body: Naomi came home saying the LORD had brought her back empty (1:21). Now the women say a son has been born to Naomi, one who "will renew your life" (v. 15). Only here does the narrator say directly that the LORD acted, giving conception (v. 13). God finished the story He had quietly been writing.

theology.title: From Ruth to David to Jesus
theology.body: The book ends with a genealogy: Obed, Jesse, David. While the judges' era fell apart, God was preparing Israel's king in a small town through a foreign widow. Matthew 1:5 names Ruth in the family line of Jesus, one of only a few women listed.

theology.title: A better Redeemer
theology.body: Boaz redeemed at a cost the nearer relative would not pay. Christians have long seen him as a picture of Christ, who became our near kinsman by taking on flesh (Hebrews 2:14–17) and paid for our redemption (Ephesians 1:7). The other relative would not risk his inheritance; Jesus gave Himself.

application.title: The man with no name
application.body: Boaz addresses the nearer relative with peloni (v. 1), roughly "so-and-so", and the narrator never names him. He protected his estate and lost his place in the story.
application.question: What are you protecting that might be keeping you out of what God is doing?

application.title: Do it in front of witnesses
application.body: Boaz settled everything at the gate before the elders. Transparency protected Ruth, the other relative and himself.
application.question: Which decision about money or family needs witnesses instead of secrecy?

application.title: Bigger than your lifetime
application.body: Ruth never knew she would be King David's great-grandmother. Her faithfulness mattered to people she would never meet.
application.question: What ordinary faithfulness this week could matter to a generation after you?
